title: Three checks and a long pause
spec: M00 · the setup that fails, then passes
intro: Run the environment check before you pull the model, so you see a real FAIL and the exact command that fixes it. Then meet the ten-to-thirty-second silence that makes every first-time reader think they broke something.
foot: Run it for real: labs-opensource/M00-dev-setup/ — python starter/check_setup.py, then python solution/hello_mistral.py

steps.title: Check first, pull second
narrative: Most setup guides tell you to install everything and then verify. Do it the other way round once: run the diagnostic on a machine that is deliberately not ready, so you find out what a failure actually looks like before you are trying to debug one at 11pm.

check_setup.py tests three things in order — the openai package imports, the Ollama server answers on localhost:11434, and the mistral model is listed. The first two pass. The third has nothing to find, because you have not pulled a model yet.

terminal.text: Fix the FAIL items above, then re-run this script.

state.label: three checks · one machine, not yet ready

cells: is any listed model name prefixed mistral?
FAIL — the tag list came back empty

view.text: A single "can't connect" error cannot tell you which of these three is wrong, and the fixes are completely different: pip install openai, ollama serve, ollama pull mistral. The script does not just report the failure — it prints the one command that clears it. That is the pattern worth stealing for your own preflight scripts.

steps.title: Pull 4 GB, then re-run
narrative: ollama pull mistral fetches roughly 4 GB of quantised weights onto your disk. This is the moment the course stops costing money — there is no API key, no per-token bill, and no request leaving your machine for the rest of the track.
Re-run the same diagnostic. Nothing changed except the third check, and now all three read [OK ]. The script exits 0 and tells you where to go next.

steps.title: The silence is the model loading
narrative: Now run the first real call. It prints two lines, and then nothing happens for ten to thirty seconds. No spinner, no progress bar, no output. Your cursor just sits there.

Nothing is broken. Ollama is reading 4 GB of weights off disk into RAM, and until that finishes there is no model to send your prompt to. The lab README states this as a gotcha in exactly those terms — first call is slow (10-30s) — because without warning, the correct instinct is to assume the connection hung and hit Ctrl-C.
Subsequent calls in the same session skip this entirely: the weights are already resident. The pause is a one-off tax, not the model's speed.
steps.youDo: python solution/hello_mistral.py — and do not hit Ctrl-C when it stalls.
steps.claudeSays: The SDK call is a normal blocking HTTP request to http://localhost:11434/v1. It has not timed out; Ollama simply has not answered yet because it is still mapping the model into memory.

⏳  (10-30 seconds of nothing — this is the part nobody warns you about)

cells: the answer appears all at once
Ollama sees no resident model, starts a cold load
~4 GB of quantised weights read from disk into RAM

views.text: Run the script a second time and the same call returns in a second or two. If you ever benchmark a local model, throw away the first measurement — you measured your SSD, not the model.

steps.title: 31 in, 34 out, and nothing billed
narrative: The response arrives with the same shape you would get from a hosted API — choices[0].message.content plus a usage block — because Ollama speaks the OpenAI wire format. That is the whole trick of this track: the code you write is portable, only the base_url changes.

The token counts are real and they are free. input: 31, output: 34 costs you electricity and RAM, not dollars — which is why the guardrail, judge and ReAct labs later in the course can afford to burn hundreds of calls in a test suite.

Your numbers will not match these. A local 7B is not deterministic across machines, and the lab says so outright: your model's exact wording and token counts will differ — that is expected. Match the shape of the output, never the exact string.
